speaker_role: student/alum (Donna, self-described MIT computer science graduate) sharing her own admitted application
commercial_incentive: None evident - personal channel, no services or products promoted
key_insights: Recommends spending significant time (she took roughly a year) writing down personal stories/experiences before drafting, so each of MIT's multiple short-answer prompts reveals a different facet of identity rather than repeating the same content

For the 'what do you do for fun' prompt, explicitly warns against writing generic answers like 'I like to volunteer,' arguing MIT wants to see authentic personal interests unconnected to resume-building

For the 'why this major/department' prompt, advises tying the choice to a specific, personal motivating story (she used a friend's cancer battle) plus concrete, school-specific detail (program language pulled from MIT's own website, with the caveat that this should support - not replace - the student's own tailored reasoning)
Advises using every single word within a school's strict word limits (100-250 words per prompt at MIT) rather than leaving space unused, since the tight limits reward maximal information density

Notes MIT's evaluators are looking for evidence a student can handle hardship/challenge (not just raw intelligence, since many applicants are valedictorians), so essays describing how the student navigated a real difficulty are valued
Mentions a college counselor's specific technique of writing 10 pages of unstructured personal reflection before selecting which stories to use across the different required essays
specific_numbers_or_facts: MIT application (at time of applicant's cycle) had roughly five short-answer prompts, word limits ranging 100-250 words each
notable_or_distinctive: A real admitted student reads and annotates her own actual MIT essays prompt-by-prompt, explaining the specific intent behind word choices and structural decisions - rare first-person transparency compared to third-party advice videos.
reliability_notes: Single self-reported success story (survivorship bias - this is what worked for one applicant in one cycle, not a guaranteed formula); MIT's specific prompts and word limits may have changed since this student's application cycle, so prompt-specific details should be verified against MIT's current application.
